LESSON 12
To Find Grace
Genesis 33:8 What meanest thou by all this drove . . . ?—the animal gifts (Genesis 32:14,15). To find grace—to win favor, to gain mercy. Esau could feel how deep and fervent was Jacob's desire.

Jacob could not come to Esau demanding his rights. By wrong action, he had forfeited all rights. He hoped only for grace, that Esau would treat him better than he deserved. This is the way we must come to God— seeking His mercy and grace. Sin has canceled any rights we may claim, but thank God! He has sent mercy. We find abundant grace in Jesus.
Esau's Rejection

Genesis 33:9-15 Esau said, I have enough, my brother—tenderness, forgiveness, and forgetfulness are here. Generosity was in his voice. My brother told Jacob that the breach between them had been closed. Jacob said . . . receive my present . . . I have seen thy face, as . . . the face of God—the great relief in Jacob's heart exaggerated Esau's kindness to a likeness of God's. Yet he acknowledged God as the cause of his blessings— God hath dealt graciously with me. God had answered his prayer. He urged him (Esau), and he took it (the gift). No doubt, both Jacob and Esau were sincere.

Esau was rejected by God as the one to carry on the covenant and to father the special nation to which Jesus was to come. Had you and I been choosing, we might have considered Esau's generous forgiving of Jacob, his cordial welcome, and unselfish treatment of him, and concluded that he deserved to be chosen. Indeed, he seems to have a greater, natural bigheartedness than did Jacob. But God does not choose men according to their natural worthiness or good traits. No one DESERVES anything from God. He has lumped all mankind together and concluded all under sin, so all may receive of His grace (Galatians 3:22). The purpose of God . . . is to stand, not of works, but of him that calleth (Romans 9:11). God looks not at how much of good or bad that the person has done, but at how he responds to God's call.

In human judgment, comparing man with man, we think surely such a one will go to Heaven for his good deeds and generosity. Yet if those deeds proceed from natural, human good nature, they are as filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6). To be acceptable with God, one's goodness must be produced by the life of God within him. That has a different quality. To be acceptable with God, our old man (self) must die, and we must become a new man in Christ Jesus.
An Altar at Shechem

Genesis 33:16-20 Esau returned to Seir, and Jacob settled at Succoth. Built him an house . . . booths for his cattle. His heavy burdens of the past wrongs were now gone, and he was ready to settle down and enjoy the blessings which God had in store for him. Later Jacob moved to Shalem, a city of Shechem, in central Canaan. He erected there an altar—continued to worship God. The name he gave it—Elelohe-Israel—indicates his personal commitment to God. "The situation of the town is one of surpassing beauty. It lies in a sheltered valley, protected by Gerizim on the south and Ebal on the north . . . It is the SYCHAR of John 4:5,6, near which the Savior conversed with the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well."—Smith's Bible Dict.
Brethren in Unity

Psalm 133:1 Good and . . . pleasant . . . for brethren to dwell . . . in unity. This meeting of the brothers is a much more pleasant picture than our previous views of them. Certainly, God was more pleased. His working in the life of Jacob was a big factor in the change, if not its sole cause.

God wills that physical brothers live in harmony. A family bound together in love and unity is a beautiful thing. Even more is it His will that His children, the Church of God, brothers and sisters in the Lord, dwell together in unity.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 13
JACOB IN CANAAN
Scripture Text: Genesis 35:1-15

Jacob followed the leading of God. Jacob cleansed his family to prepare to worship God. We must be clean before our worship is acceptable. Jacob worshiped where God first appeared to him. It is good to remember our experiences with God. God blessed Jacob again. God wants to bless us if we will let Him.

Jacob realized that cleanness and holiness are necessary to please a holy God. While he had continued to worship God since committing his life to Him at Bethel years before, yet he had become somewhat slack and allowed worship of images and use of charms in his family. To be fit to meet God in worship, they must be rid of these. God accepts no mixed worship.
MEMORY VERSE: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God. —Matthew 5:8
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 45 The sin of worshiping images.
Tue.—2 Corinthians 6:14-18; Isaiah 52:1-11 To worship God, one must separate from sin.
Wed.—Deuteronomy 6:1-12 Saints' responsibility to pass on God's Law to their children.
Thu.—Ephesians 6:1-9 Parents and children relationship.
Fri.—John 5:19-29 Jesus example of father, son relationship.
Devotional Reading: Psalm 115 The sin of trust in idols.
Put Away the Strange Gods

Genesis 35:1-4 Jacob and his family had lived in Canaan for some time (since coming from Padanaram) when God spoke to him in a command. Go up to Bethel. Make there an altar. Why there? Because there God appeared unto thee when thou fleddest from . . . Esau (Genesis 28:10-22). The memory was dear to God as well as to Jacob. He wanted Jacob to have the blessing which going back there would be. Jacob said unto his household, and to all—he was responsible for those in his care—Put away the strange gods—images, idols, probably brought in from Padanaram—be clean—morally clean from sin—change your garments—a physical cleanness as a symbol of the moral cleanness. Let us go up to Bethel . . . make . . . an altar unto God, who answered me . . . was with me—Jacob was remembering and measuring up to that mercy. They gave unto Jacob all the strange gods . . . their earrings—earrings were put in the same category as strange gods. Why? Because they were objects of superstitious trust to protect from evil powers, giving to them glory that rightfully belonged to God. Jacob hid them under the oak—buried them.
He and All the People

Genesis 35:5-8 The terror of God was upon the cities . . . and they did not pursue—God protected Jacob from the fierce people of Canaan. Jacob came to . . . Bethel, he and all the people . . . with him—took his entire household into the worship. Built there an altar, and called the place El-bethel—an addition to the name given before. El means God and El-bethel means the God of the house of God. The altar was a memorial of the time God appeared unto him while he slept on the ground, when he fled from the face of his brother.

Jacob did not go alone. He included his family and servants in his worship. Are we content to worship alone while the children go their own ways? Would we eat our fill while the family went hungry or sleep comfortably

LESSON 13

in a warm bed while the children wandered in the rain and cold? The best of all blessings is to know God and to worship Him in Spirit and in Truth. Let us not keep these to ourselves but do our best to bring them in.
God Appears Unto Jacob Again

Genesis 35:9-15 God appeared unto Jacob again . . . and blessed him. God came down and talked with Jacob. We know this because he went up from him (verse 13). He repeated the promise made before of many descendants and of giving Canaan to him and his seed, adding, kings shall come out of thy loins. The greatest of these is the King of kings, Jesus. Jacob set up a pillar of stone, as he had done the first time (Genesis 28:18). He poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon—setting it apart as sacred to God.

After lingering at Bethel where Rebekah's nurse died, they moved on to near Bethlehem, where Benjamin was born and Rachel died, to Edar, and on to Mamre—the plains of Mamre (Genesis 18:1) in southern Canaan, to the city of Hebron. Here in Hebron, Jacob's grandfather, Abraham, had lived, and now his father, Isaac, lived here.

Jacob's past experience was not enough. Its influence was fading until he was allowing images, etc., in his house. He needed to be drawn back. He needed, as we do, a continuing contact with God. By continual prayer, Bible study, fellowship with the saints, worship and service of God, our souls are kept flourishing, our love fresh, our hearts tender, and our lives pure. Not what we were in the past, but what we are now is what counts. He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved (Matthew 24:13).
Called the Name Bethel

One cannot meet God and ever be the same again. Always to be dear to Jacob's heart was Bethel, the place of a permanent change in his life, the place where he first met God. God had led him to return to his land (Genesis 31:13) and now to worship again at this place, this very spot. The ideal which had there been born in his heart impelled him to cleanse his family of wrong practices to measure to the standard set then.

Let us never forget the God-stirred emotions which accompanied our salvation. Looking back to that time and tasting again of that holy joy, many a one has been strengthened to overcome temptation, trial or discouragement. The memory of that hour brings a renewed determination.
Jacob would later reap the seeds of deception which he sowed in his brother, Esau, through his ten older sons in their selling of their brother, Joseph.
JUST A THOUGHT
It's a lot more fun to stop adding up your troubles and to start counting your blessings.

He repeated the promise made before of many descendants and of giving Canaan to him and his seed, adding, kings shall come out of thy loins.
The greatest of these is the King of kings, Jesus.
Jacob set up a pillar of stone, as he had done the first time (Genesis 28:18).
He poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon—setting it apart as sacred to God.

After lingering at Bethel where Rebekah's nurse died, they moved on to near Bethlehem, where Benjamin was born and Rachel died, to Edar, and on to Mamre—the plains of Mamre (Genesis 18:1) in southern Canaan, to the city of Hebron.
Here in Hebron, Jacob's grandfather, Abraham, had lived, and now his father, Isaac, lived here.
Jacob's past experience was not enough.
Its influence was fading until he was allowing images, etc., in his house.
He needed to be drawn back.
He needed, as we do, a continuing contact with God.
By continual prayer, Bible study, fellowship with the saints, worship and service of God, our souls are kept flourishing, our love fresh, our hearts tender, and our lives pure.
Not what we were in the past, but what we are now is what counts.
He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved (Matthew 24:13).
One cannot meet God and ever be the same again.
Always to be dear to Jacob's heart was Bethel, the place of a permanent change in his life, the place where he first met God.
God had led him to return to his land (Genesis 31:13) and now to worship again at this place, this very spot.
The ideal which had there been born in his heart impelled him to cleanse his family of wrong practices to measure to the standard set then.
Let us never forget the God-stirred emotions which accompanied our salvation.
Looking back to that time and tasting again of that holy joy, many a one has been strengthened to overcome temptation, trial or discouragement.
The memory of that hour brings a renewed determination.
Jacob would later reap the seeds of deception which he sowed in his brother, Esau, through his ten older sons in their selling of their brother, Joseph.
It's a lot more fun to stop adding up your troubles and to start counting your blessings.

lines.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 1
GOD CALLS ABRAHAM
Scripture Texts: Genesis 12:1-8; Genesis 13:14-17; Hebrews 11:8-10
God has always had a plan. He also has always had a need for a man
to carry out His plan. In this lesson Abraham is that man. Abraham
believed God. He obeyed God. He looked forward in faith to God's
Kingdom. His faith was his righteousness. Abraham built an altar
everywhere he went.
Throughout Old Testament history, God made things happen as
examples to us. They are types. They teach spiritual Truths. God had
them written for our learning, our warning. We are the ones upon
whom the ends of the world are come, or the time of the last
dispensation, the Gospel age. These lessons are specifically for us. If we
were to have a text for this quarter, it would be found in 1 Corinthians
10:11: Now all these things happened unto them for examples: and
they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the
world are come.
MEMORY VERSE: And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
—Genesis 15:6
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 11:10-32 Abraham's family.
Tue.—Joshua 24:1-13 God's dealings with Abraham & Isaac.
Wed.—Nehemiah 9:5-15 God keeps His promises.
Thu.—Psalm 119:1-16 Obedience to God's Word.
Fri.—Isaiah 51:1-8 God's promise of everlasting salvation.
Devotional Reading: Romans 4 The everlasting covenant of faith.
Get Thee Out
Genesis 12:1-4 God works through men. He has chosen to use a man, woman, boy or girl to carry out His
plan. Blessed is the one who obeys and is used. Abraham was such a man. The Lord had said—before this time
(Genesis 11:31). Terah, Abraham's father, appears to have been in accord with the command of God and to have
obeyed. The command was: Get thee out of thy country . . . unto a land that I will shew thee. Terah had led
the family from Ur to Haran.
God promised to make of Abraham a great nation, a great name and a blessing. He would bless all
families of the earth through him. We know now that this blessing was Christ Who was born as a human
descendant of Abraham. Enemies of Abraham were to be cursed and friends blessed. His history and that of
Israel shows that these promises were all fulfilled.
Abraham lived some 1900 years B.C. He had to leave Ur, where idolatry and other sins were practiced,
before God could fully use him. Separation from our old lives of sin, from associates, and from any element that
may influence us away from God's way is necessary. We may not need to move our home or change our
employment, but there must be a total change in our inner lives. There will be new connection with God, new
loves, new beliefs, new purposes, new goals, new thoughts and actions, new virtues, new hopes, a new Leader, a
new source of spiritual food, and in all things a new life. Abram departed, as the Lord had spoken unto him.
He believed enough to act accordingly.

LESSON 1
Abraham Builded an Altar
Genesis 12:5-8 Abraham obeyed God and went on into the land of Canaan. Again, the Lord appeared
unto Abram. He promised to give this land unto Abram's seed. At each place Abram settled, he builded an
altar unto the Lord. He burned sacrifices to God and worshiped Him.
This is one secret of Abraham's faithfulness and the good character of his family. Worship of God was the
center of his home life. Daily family worship is one of the strongest powers for good a people can possess. Its
lack is an irreparable loss.
Abraham's Seed to Be Without Number
Genesis 13:14-17 Lift up now thine eyes, and look . . . the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it.
The borders of this land were from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates (Genesis
15:18). God promised Abraham's seed (his descendants) to be as the dust of the earth—an innumerable
multitude. This is the way God gave the land. However, there were conditions, or strings, attached
(Deuteronomy 28). The belief that the land of Canaan was given to literal Israel unconditionally and to be
certainly occupied by the Jews is incorrect. Rather, Deuteronomy 28:63-64 has been fulfilled because of the
sins of the people, just as God warned. God has no special favors for the literal Jewish nation in this
dispensation. God's interest and promises are now to a new Canaan and a new Israel. This is a spiritual people, a
spiritual nation, The Church of God.
A City That Hath Foundations
Hebrews 11:8-10 By faith Abraham . . . obeyed . . . went . . . not knowing whither. It took faith to leave
the known for the unknown—and at the age of seventy-five. Read Hebrews 11:1. Faith made it real to
Abraham, gave him a real and certain goal to work toward. He believed God. His faith enabled him to live
temporarily in a strange country throughout his earthly life, to live as a stranger, a foreigner. Saints are
strangers in this land; they are citizens of another country—Heaven. For he looked for a city which hath
foundations, a permanent city. It would be permanent and good because its builder and maker is God. This is
no earthly city. It is the Kingdom of God which Jesus later set up. Abraham was not privileged to see it. But,
thanks be to God, we have found it. We can see it. Salvation gives us a residence in it.
The city Abraham looked for is founded on something more sure than material stones. The things which
are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18). By faith,
Abraham looked down the centuries and saw the Kingdom of God, the church, eternal, that cannot be destroyed,
that the gates of hell shall not prevail against (Matthew 16:18), because it is built on the Rock, Christ Jesus.
With that vision in his heart, earth lost its appeal. He saw something better. The trials and hardships of this life
were bearable. Faith in his heart reached up to God and fastened onto that which was only a promise as yet.
Abraham was one of the greatest men in the Bible. Why? His greatness was not so much in doing as in
believing, not so much in leading as in following. He knew how to obey. He stood firm in his believing. He did
not blindly follow just any voice. The same will be ours if we believe and obey the Lord.
Our Great Privilege
We have received the reality of which Abraham had but the promise. Christ has come and made atonement
for sin. He has set up His Kingdom in many hearts. He has sent the Holy Spirit to indwell them. These blessings
are in the church today. They give us greater resources for living steadfast in the Lord than Abraham had. Are
you taking advantage of these privileges provided in God's plan of salvation?

LESSON 2
GOD'S COVENANT WITH ABRAHAM
Scripture Texts: Genesis 17:1-10; Galatians 3:7-10, 14
God called out Abraham for a purpose. We see something of that purpose
today as we study of the covenant He made with Abraham. God intends these
accounts of Abraham and others to be examples to us. If we study them
rightfully for the purpose of avoiding the errors and gaining the virtues, we
can profit much spiritually.
God established an everlasting covenant with Abraham. God was to be a
God to Abraham and his seed. By faith, Abraham received the promise from
God to him and his family. By faith, we are receivers of the promise made to
Abraham to send the Holy Spirit.
MEMORY VERSE: So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.
—Galatians 3:9
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 15 God's covenant with Abraham.
Tue.—Genesis 17:9-27 The covenant of circumcision.
Wed.—Romans 2:17-29 The Jews guilty before God.
Thu.—Acts 7:1-8 Stephen recounts the covenant.
Fri.—Luke 1:68-80 Zacharias sings of the fulfilling of the covenant.
Devotional Reading: Galatians 3:6-29 Faith in Christ is entrance to covenant.
Be Thou Perfect
Genesis 17:1 Abram was ninety years old and nine. All his long life, God had been bringing him to a
place where He could have him to Himself. Walk before me, and be thou perfect. This is God's eternal
standard for all of us. Over nineteen hundred years later Jesus said, Be ye therefore perfect, even as your
Father which is in heaven is perfect (Matthew 5:48).
There is much opposition in the thinking of our day to the possibility of any man being perfect. It is true that
we cannot be perfect in knowledge, strength or ability, or as other men see us. Yet in purity of heart, God
requires perfection—perfect in His eyes because He sees in our hearts. Since He requires it, it is possible,
possible because He furnishes all that is needed for heart perfection. Jesus Christ cleanses the heart from sin and
provides the power through the Holy Spirit.
Fell on His Face
Genesis 17:2-3 I will make my covenant between me and thee. It is a marvelous thing that God will stoop
to covenant with man. It raises man to a much higher plain. Will multiply thee—many descendants for
Abraham. Abraham fell on his face—in submission, respect and honor, humility, worship—and God talked
with him.
Abraham here displayed the attitude necessary for entering into fellowship with God and for receiving His
best gifts. We must yield; give up ourselves and our will to Him. We must take the lowest place before Him
Who has the highest place.

LESSON 2
A New Name
Genesis 17:4-6 God repeats His promise of a covenant and descendants. Neither shall thy name any more
be called Abram, but thy name . . . Abraham—a name with much greater meaning because of a changed
status. I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee. The greatest of these kings is Jesus,
humanly descended from Abraham.
This Covenant Was Everlasting
Genesis 17:7-10 An everlasting covenant—not for a short time or a few people only. It was to hold
throughout all time. God would be a God, not only to Abraham, but to his seed. I will give unto thee and to thy
seed . . . all the land of Canaan. It was not God Who broke this promise. Israel later did not obey the
conditions. See Deuteronomy 28:58-64; 1 Kings 9:6-7.
Let us give careful attention to this promise. The same blessing promised to Abraham is for us today. Christ
died that we might receive it—the promise of the Spirit. God promised three things: (1) many nations as
descendants, (2) to be a God to Abraham and his seed, and (3) to give Canaan to Abraham and his seed. All that
is provided for us in this Gospel dispensation. This is God's part. Thou shalt keep my covenant . . . thou, and
thy seed. This is man's part. That covenant was not limited to what was covered by the Law. The Law covenant
was given later because of man's weakness, because men needed to learn that they cannot become righteous by
their own efforts, that they must have the cleansing and the power of God. God's promise to Abraham was given
before the Law, and it reaches beyond the Law (Romans 4:13-16). The Spirit was sent to abide forever on the
Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:1-21).
All May Be Children of Abraham
Galatians 3:7-10 They which are of faith—those who believe God—the same are the children of
Abraham. Here this covenant is carried over into the New Testament dispensation. To thy seed after thee.
Who are the seed? Not those related in the flesh, but those related in spirit. The children of Abraham now are
those saved from sin by faith in Jesus Christ. This salvation through Christ, this gospel, was preached before ...
unto Abraham. God referred to the Gospel of Christ when He said; In thee shall all nations be blessed. The
just shall live by faith, not by the Law.
Galatians 3:14 That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles—God provides that we all—
no one left out—may have the same blessing promised to Abraham. This is to be obtained through Jesus
Christ. He purchased it for us by His death, by taking upon Himself the curse (verse 13). That we might
receive the promise. What promise? The promise of the Spirit received through faith. The Spirit was sent to
abide forever (John 14:16).
Abraham believed the promise but died without receiving its fulfillment (Hebrews 11:13). The fulfillment
came with the death of Christ and the coming of the Holy Spirit. It is ours today, but many people are missing
all or part of it because of not exercising faith in it. Let us all believe and receive it. Then spread the good news.
JUST A THOUGHT
To be lied about when one is innocent
is preferable to having the truth told when one is guilty.

LESSON 3
ABRAHAM AND HIS THREE VISITORS
Scripture Text: Genesis 18
In the days before God had given a written Bible, He spoke to men
audibly. On some special occasions, He appeared to them, as in today's
lesson.
Three men came to Abraham. One was Jesus Christ. The other two
were types of the Word and Spirit in the form of angels. Abraham
welcomed them. The Lord promised to send Isaac. Commanding one's
children to do right permits God to bless them. God cannot bear sin.
Prayer changes things.
We may think the command to be hospitable to be a small matter of
importance. Yet it is God's command and to be obeyed. Abraham would
have missed great blessings if he had not opened his home and heart to
these visitors. Can you tell instances when the sharing of comforts with
wayfarers may have brought the giving or receiving of rich and far-
reaching blessings, perhaps the saving of souls?
MEMORY VERSE: Ah Lord God! Behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and
stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee.
—Jeremiah 32:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 13 Abraham's generosity to Lot.
Tue.—Jeremiah 32:16-25 Jeremiah's prayer.
Wed.—Jeremiah 32:26-40 The Lord's answer to his prayer.
Thu.—Psalm 25 A prayer of trust.
Fri.—Psalm 65 Living in communion with God.
Devotional Reading: Luke 18:1-8 Jesus teaches importunity in prayer.
God Promises Abraham a Son
Genesis 18:1-15 The Lord appeared unto him—to Abraham. This undoubtedly was the Son, later named
Jesus—it was the Lord. Three men stood by him . . . he ran to meet them . . . bowed himself . . . And said ...
pass not away . . . Abraham gave them a welcome. He was hospitable, as we are commanded to be (1 Peter
4:9). No doubt, this is the reference in Hebrews 13:2. Abraham furnished them water to wash their feet, and
food—cakes, meat, butter, and milk. Abraham went to much inconvenience to show hospitality to the men.
Where is Sarah thy wife? Her name had recently been changed from Sarai—meaning my princess—to
Sarah, princess (Genesis 17:15). She no longer belonged to Abraham only. She was mother of a nation. Sarah
thy wife shall have a son. Sarah, ninety years old, thought it impossible. She laughed within herself. Abraham
had also laughed (Genesis 17:17) when, shortly before, he had been given the same promise. Man's small,
limited mind finds it difficult to comprehend the greatness of God's power. But, Is anything too hard for the
LORD? No, nothing! (Luke 1:37.) Then the Lord repeated the promise to send Isaac. It was certain and sure.
Isaac was a necessary part of His plan to carry on the covenant.
Sarah was hidden in the tent behind the Lord. She did not laugh aloud but inwardly. She thought He would
not know. It frightened her that He did know. Then she denied. Still, He knew. Are we like Sarah sometimes,
thinking we can hide something from God? This is impossible. She thought what God said was impossible.
© 2015 Church of God, Inc.

LESSON 3
Judgment of Sodom
Genesis 18:16-31 The men rose up—the Lord and two angels (see Genesis 18:22 and Genesis 19:1). They
looked toward Sodom, where Lot lived, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 13:11-13). Abraham counted it a
privilege to walk a part of the way with them. As they walked, the Lord considered whether He should tell
Abraham His purpose concerning Sodom. He found no reason not to. Abraham was to become a great . . .
nation, all nations were to be blessed in him, and he would command his children . . . after him to do right.
Therefore, He decided to tell Abraham.
Abraham was to become a great and mighty nation. This was dependent upon how he raised his children.
God knew he would command them after him. He would teach them what he knew of the Lord. He would not
only teach them, but he would train them so they would keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and
judgment in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken.
The future of any people rests in its children. It is without question that our great nation, America, is taking
the downward way. The tide could yet be turned by the general practice of DAILY FAMILY WORSHIP and by
both TEACHING and TRAINING the children to keep the way of the LORD. One may not be able to make it
general, but each of us is responsible for the children under our influence.
The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great . . . their sin is very grievous. God notices what people do.
What people do is dictated by the condition of the heart. God cannot bear to look at sin. Sin stirs God's wrath. I
will go down now, and see—to see if the cry rightly represented the sin of the cities. The men . . . went toward
Sodom. The two angels were God's agents to investigate. They were a type of the Word and the Spirit of God.
Without them, souls cannot be drawn and led out of sin and destruction. The angels had business in Sodom—to
draw people out of the destruction which God would bring on the sin and division. The Lord had business with
Abraham. He abides. He knew Abraham's heart and his concern for Lot who dwelt in Sodom. Standing together,
while the angels left on their mission to Sodom, the Lord showed Abraham His plan to destroy the wicked cities.
Abraham pled with the Lord for the righteous that might be in Sodom. He reasoned that they should not be
destroyed with the wicked. His plea to the Lord was to spare the place if fifty righteous be found there. He
continued pleading, lowering the number to forty-five, and then on down to ten.
For Ten's Sake
Genesis 18:32-33 Peradventure ten shall be found there. The Lord granted each request. I will not
destroy it for ten's sake. The Lord did not stop granting, but there Abraham stopped asking. What a lesson on
prayer we have here—(1) the value of perseverance (James 5:16), (2) the loving mercy of God in hearing and
granting requests, and (3) the responsibility of saints to pray, since so much power is carried by prayer. Notice
upon what God allowed the fate of thousands of wicked people to depend—the prayers of one righteous man.
Were ten found? No. What might have been the result had Abraham spoken yet once more and asked for
FOUR? How many are dependent upon our faithfulness and persistent prayers?
JUST A THOUGHT
Marriage is often a case where cupidity meets stupidity.

LESSON 4
THE DESTRUCTION OF SODOM
Scripture Text: Genesis 19:1-29
Today we study a continuation of last week's lesson in which
Sodom's destruction was forecast. God punishes sin, and He protects
His people. It is a mistake to raise children in sinful surroundings.
We must obey God in all circumstances. Then He will answer prayer.
There is little in the record of Lot to justify God's remembering
him, but because of the overflow of Abraham's life, Lot was saved,
and he was brought out of Sodom safely. There is one assurance to
which a Christian can look to when he is saved. He can contribute to
the community in which he lives by the overflow of righteousness
from his life. Everyone either raises or lowers the moral and spiritual
standards of the home, church, or community in which he is a part.
MEMORY VERSE: Remember Lot's wife.
—Luke 17:32
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 1:1-20 A call to repentance.
Tue.—Ezekiel 16:44-59 Sodom, classic example of sin.
Wed.—Luke 17:24-37 The end will be as the days of Lot.
Thu.—Romans 1:18-32 Sin deserves God's wrath.
Fri.—2 Peter 2:4-17 The righteous judgments of God.
Devotional Reading: Ezekiel 18:20-32 God's fair judgments.
Flee Temptation
Genesis 19:1-3 There came two angels to Sodom—are not these the two "men" who visited Abraham in
company with the Lord and who went toward Sodom? (Genesis 18:22.) Lot sat in the gate—a public and
official gathering place. He was well known in Sodom. Lot . . . rose up . . . bowed himself—showed respect
and hospitality. He pressed upon them—urged them—they . . . entered into his house; and he made them a
feast— maybe not as yet realizing they were not ordinary men.
Lot's mistake was in choosing to live in a wicked place. Some of his children were lost with Sodom. Unless
we flee temptation and abstain from all appearance of evil, we cannot ask God to protect us from sin's painful
influences. It was Abraham whom God remembered and answered, not Lot.
These lessons should have an alarming effect upon us now. The signs in our land indicate an approach
toward the spiritual and moral degradation of Sodom. We cannot hope for our land to wake up and turn to God.
The lost do not save themselves. Sodom's hope lay in the presence of but ten righteous and the prayers of one.
The task of turning the tide in our land rests upon those who know God. What can we do? (1) Live sanctified
lives. (2) Carry a burden and pray much. (3) Spread the Gospel of Christ everywhere. (4) Teach and train the
children to live godly. (5) Combat evil forces by every possible means.
This Fellow Came in to Sojourn
Genesis 19:4-11 Before they lay down—they lost no time—the men of Sodom, compassed the house
round—formed a mob. Old and young . . . from every quarter—they represented the whole city, not realizing
they were demonstrating what the angels came to learn. Where are the men . . . ? bring them out—degraded,

LESSON 4
sinful, and brutal mistreatment was planned. When Lot pled with them to do not so wickedly, they threatened
him. This one . . . came in to sojourn—an outsider living there temporarily—yet was trying to judge, or
command, them. They pressed sore upon Lot and came near to break the door. Lot was in danger. The
people were wicked and violent in their degenerate condition. The power of sin had a terrible hold upon them.
But God was watching. Abraham had prayed for Lot. Lot was still righteous, but very foolish and unwise (2
Peter 2:7-8). The men (angels) . . . pulled Lot into the house . . . shut to the door . . . smote the men . . . with
blindness, so they could not find the door. This was a miracle and an evidence that they were not natural
humans. They were supernatural. They were angels. They used God's power.
When God's Word and the Holy Spirit are brought before sinners, it calls for action. People will either be
sarcastic, ridicule, and threaten, or they will receive that which they represent. The saint does not answer the
sinner on his level; this only leads to quarreling. Truth and holiness are his weapons and are mighty through
God to the pulling down of strong holds (2 Corinthians 10:4). Lot was humanly no match for the mob, but
God's power used by the angels put them to defeat. To show this kind of attitude toward God's messengers
always brings spiritual blindness. God's true messengers are His Word and His Spirit.
As One That Mocked
Genesis 19:12-23 The men said unto Lot, Hast thou here any . . . son in law . . . sons . . . daughters . . .
bring them out. They were searching for the righteous—those ten or more—for all who would believe and
obey. We will destroy this place . . . the cry of them is . . . great before . . . the Lord—God was stirred. Lot
. . . spake unto his sons in law . . . Up, get you out . . . the Lord will destroy this city. But he seemed as one
that mocked—they did not believe him, thought he was fooling. In the morning the angels hastened Lot . . .
take thy wife, and thy two daughters—FOUR, not ten. While he lingered—in no hurry to leave though
destruction was so near. Hurry out of sin while there is still time! The men laid hold upon his hand and the
hands of the others—great urgency. The Lord showed great mercy unto them. They set him without the city.
He said, Escape . . . look not behind thee—don't look back. God's commands are to be obeyed. Yet through all
this, Lot desired to bargain with God, to work some of his own will into God's plan.
Why did Lot's sons-in-law not believe him? It would appear his previous life had been lacking in concern for
his family. Possibly, he was partly responsible for their present condition. It pays to live at all times so that we
can draw upon God's strength in times of crisis. It pays to so live that our family has confidence in our words.
The Awful Penalty of Sin
Genesis 19:24-29 Then the Lord rained upon Sodom . . . brimstone and fire—the awful penalty of sin—
DEATH. The cities, people, everything all destroyed. God means what He says. But his wife looked back.
When leaving sin, the future is bright and good; sin has nothing worth looking back to. See Luke 9:62. She
became a pillar of salt—again, the penalty of sin. God told us to remember this. Abraham got up early—his
concern was great and real—to where he stood before the Lord—where the day before he had prayed for
Sodom to be spared. Looked toward . . . the smoke . . . went up as the smoke of a furnace—a tragic sight, the
result of sin. Was Abraham's prayer ignored? No, God heard and granted even more than asked. God
remembered Abraham. Ten righteous were not found, but He sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow.
His goodness and mercy are everlasting.
Does the punishment of Lot's wife seem too severe? We must learn that sin is exceedingly sinful. Remember
that these things happened unto them for our examples (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Peter 2:6). They are important
because of that of which they are types.

LESSON 5
THE BIRTH OF ISAAC
Scripture Texts: Genesis 21:1-12; Galatians 4:22-31
God's plan for Abraham was moving forward. The time came for Him to
fulfill His promise of a son for Abraham.
God sent Isaac as promised. Ishmael mocked Isaac and was sent away.
Ishmael is a type of people under the Law, the Old Testament covenant. If we
live after the flesh, we are children of the bondwoman. Isaac is a type of people
under the Gospel of Christ, the new covenant. If we live after the Spirit, we are
children of the freewoman.
MEMORY VERSE: Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise.
—Galatians 4:28
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 16 Birth of Ishmael.
Tue.—Luke 1:54-79 The covenant being fulfilled.
Wed.—Genesis 20 Abraham's deception.
Thu.—Genesis 21:12-21 God's care for Ishmael.
Fri.—John 8:31-40 Abraham's seed counted spiritually.
Devotional Reading: Romans 9:14-33 God's righteousness, mercy.
God Keeps His Promises
Genesis 21:1-7 The Lord visited Sarah as he had said— God always keeps His Word. Abraham was an
hundred years old, Sarah was ninety, and Ishmael was fourteen. Abraham called the name of his son . . .
Isaac—the name God had given in Genesis 17:19. It means laughter. Both Abraham and Sarah had laughed
when hearing the promise of a son in old age. Abraham circumcised . . . Isaac . . . as God had commanded in
Genesis 17:10-14—the ordinance which symbolically bound them in covenant with God.
Circumcision was the ordinance God gave as a seal of the covenant He made with Abraham. Since Isaac was
to carry on the covenant, he, too, was circumcised, as all his sons were to be. It is an everlasting covenant
(Genesis 17:19). Circumcision also continues, not as a physical rite, but in the spiritual life the ordinance
symbolizes. Until Christ came, it was circumcision of the flesh. Since He brought the Gospel, it is circumcision
of the heart, made without hands. It is putting off . . . the sins of the flesh (Colossians 2:11). It is holiness of
life. Before Christ, one who was not circumcised was cut off from his people for breaking the covenant
(Genesis 17:14). Now those who are not cleansed from sin and made new creatures in Christ are cut off from
God's people (Galatians 6:15).
A Casting Out
Genesis 21:8-11 Abraham made a . . . feast—celebrating the first step of progress Isaac had made—
weaning. Sarah saw the son of Hagar . . . mocking—the son of her servant woman exulting over her free son
Isaac, this son of God's promise. Irritated, Sarah said . . . Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son
. . . shall not be heir with my son. Not only Ishmael's presence bothered her, but the prospect of his equality in
inheritance from Abraham, father of both him and Isaac. The thing was very grievous to Abraham. Why?
Because he loved Ishmael.

This was grievous to the heart of Abraham because Ishmael was his son also, and it gave him pain to cast
him out. For the plan of God to be followed in our lives as He would have it, we will find, many times, things
that must be cast out of our lives which lay close to our hearts. Similarly, it gives God pain to cast out any of His
created people. He loves them all. He is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). But the choice lies
with us. Unless we repent, we are outside of God's family (Luke 13:3).
Isaac in God's Plan
Genesis 21:12 God said unto Abraham . . . in all that Sarah hath said . . . hearken unto her. It was
God's will that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away—for in Isaac shall thy seed be called. God's special plan was
to be carried on through Isaac, not Ishmael.
Galatians 4:22-23 Abraham had two sons—but they were different. They had different mothers, one a
bondwoman and one a freewoman. A son is of the same substance as his parent. Ishmael was born after the
flesh—just a human, earthly, carnal child. Isaac was born by promise—God promised to send him. God had a
purpose which, having begun in Abraham was to proceed on through Isaac, on in an ever-progressing plan
through his seed, to come to fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The Two Covenants
Genesis 21:24-31 Which things are an allegory—a type. They are symbolic, figurative. They mean
something further than the material happenings. These—the bondwoman Hagar and the freewoman Sarah—are
the two covenants. One covenant is that given from the mount Sinai—the Law which was given to Moses on
that mountain. The Law gendereth to bondage—it brought a curse because it showed man his sin but had no
power to free him from it. Which is Agar—Agar (Hagar) was a type of the Law covenant, or agreement. This
Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to—corresponds to, or is a type of Jerusalem which now is—
the capital city of the Jews where the temple was, from which the Law of Moses was administered. This earthly
Jerusalem, which stood for the Law, was in bondage with her children, the Jews, followers of the Law.
Ishmael is a type of followers of the Law. Still, in our present day, all who cling to the works of the Law are in
bondage (Galatians 3:10-11; Romans 3:20).
But Jerusalem which is above—the heavenly capital city, the church of the living God, from which the
Law of Christ, the Gospel, is administered—is free, which is the mother of us all. The church is the mother of
all the saved, of all those living under the Gospel, set free from the law of sin and death (Romans 8:2-4). Sarah
was a type of the Gospel covenant or agreement.
Two Sons Were Very Different
Isaac and Ishmael were very different. They were born of different mothers. Their lives and destinies were
different. They were treated differently. These things are written for our admonition. They apply to us. There
are two kinds of people in the world—saved and unsaved, saints and sinners. There is a difference in people
living in their own human strength and those living by the power of God. They are born of different sources—
one kind after the flesh, the other after the Spirit. They live differently—one kind in sin, the other in holiness.
Their natures are different—one kind has the carnal nature, the other, the divine nature. Their destinies are
different—one kind is headed for hell, the other for Heaven. Dear ones, which kind of people are you? Make
your calling and election sure.

LESSON 6
ABRAHAM SACRIFICES ISAAC
Scripture Text: Genesis 22:1-18
Abraham had shown faithfulness to God, but a greater test was
coming. He must be proven worthy of the place God had for him to fill.
Abraham obeyed God. He gave his best to God. He had complete faith in
God. Abraham offered Isaac as a sacrifice, realizing that God would
handle the rest. Isaac is a type of Christ Who was offered by His Father as
a sacrifice for our sins.
The ram was a substitute for Isaac. By its death, Isaac received his life
back again. Thus the ram became a type of Christ Who was to die as a
substitute for sinners? By His substitutionary death, Christ gave life to all
who received Him. God blesses those who obey Him.
MEMORY VERSE: By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up
Isaac: and he that had received the promises offered up his only
begotten son.
—Hebrews 11:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—James 2:14-26 True faith evidenced by works.
Tue.—Genesis 23 Death and burial of Sarah.
Wed.—Genesis 25:7-18 The death of Abraham.
Thu.—Luke 16:22-31 Abraham in Paradise.
Fri.—Leviticus 22:17-25 A perfect sacrifice required.
Devotional Reading: Hebrews 11:8-19 Abraham's faith and obedience.
Abraham Rose Up Early and Went
Genesis 22:1-3 God did tempt Abraham—did not tempt him with evil, for God never does that (James
1:13). This was a test to prove Abraham. Take now thy son—Josephus says Isaac was twenty-five at this
time—thine only son Isaac—there was Ishmael, another son, but he was son of a bondwoman. Isaac was the
only son of Sarah, the freewoman, only son of promise, the only one to carry forward the covenant of God. Get
thee into the land of Moriah. This land was probably the land of Mt. Moriah in the east part of Jerusalem.
Offer him there for a burnt offering—as they sacrificed animals to God. Abraham rose up early . . . and
went—no putting it off, arguing, evading, or doubting. He simply obeyed, and promptly—early.
This command is hard to understand without knowing the result. It seems against God's purpose in Isaac,
seems to overthrow the good of His covenant with man. But we only see here a part of His plan. Abraham also
saw but part. He had only the command, no explanation. Why then did he obey so wholeheartedly? Because one
thing was above all others to him— the will of God. If God said to sacrifice Isaac, Abraham wanted to do it,
even though it was hard. He obeyed. He got up early and went all the way.
Abraham Went All the Way
Genesis 22:4-10 Then on the third day . . . saw the place afar off. He had traveled three days, and here he
left his servants behind. He and Isaac, with the wood for the burnt offering, would go the rest of the way
alone. But notice here the great faith that Abraham shows. Here his faith in God really comes to the front. Abide

ye here . . . I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you. Talk about faith! He said they
would both come back.
Abraham took the wood . . . laid it upon Isaac his son . . . the fire . . . a knife; and they went both of
them together—together. See the strong relationship here, father and son bound together in a deep fellowship
with God. Isaac had to be willing also. Here is a type of the Cross laid upon Jesus. Isaac spake . . . where is the
lamb? A hard question. It must have struck deep into Abraham's heart. He could not yet bear to tell Isaac all the
instructions, because he did not have all the answers. But this much he did know, God will provide himself a
lamb. He did not know how. No doubt he thought of Isaac as the one God had provided. His words were truer
than he knew.
They came to the place . . . Abraham built an altar there . . . bound Isaac . . . laid him on the altar . . .
took the knife—they obeyed to the last move. In Abraham's heart and mind and purpose, Isaac was already
dead. In a moment he would be, in fact.
God will provide himself a lamb. God uses Abraham's words to point down through the centuries to Jesus
Christ, the Lamb of God Whom He provided as an offering for the sins of the world. In this incident, Isaac was a
type of Christ. As Abraham gave his son, his dearest possession, so God was to give His greater Son. Isaac and
the ram together completed a perfect type of Christ's sacrifice.
Abraham Passes the Test
Genesis 22:11-14 Angel of the Lord called . . . Abraham, Abraham: and he said, Here am I—right
there in the path of obedience. Lay not thine hand upon the lad—God did not intend the actual death of Isaac.
Now I know that thou fearest God. The test was over. God found Abraham's heart to be perfect; he had passed
the test. Thou hast not withheld thy son—Abraham gave his best to God. God requires the same from us—no
withholding. Abraham . . . looked, and behold . . . a ram— God's provision in plenty of time, but not a minute
early. Abraham . . . took the ram, and offered him up—a substitute. Imagine the joy of father and son in that
worship, yes, of God also. No grief now, no conflict, no question. How bound together in one were these three!
Perhaps nowhere does the faith of Abraham shine more brightly than in this test. His wonderful obedience
had a cause. Its roots were in his faith. He believed God's plans were all good, that His ability was perfect, and
that His will would be carried out to a perfect end. His belief went beyond the natural. He believed God was
able to raise Isaac up, even from the dead (Hebrews 11:19), and give him seed as promised. He did not ask
how or why. In his thinking, he already killed Isaac before he had quite carried it out. He received him back
from the dead, in a figure.
Obedience Brings Blessings
Genesis 22:15-18 The angel of the Lord called . . . because thou hast . . . not withheld thy son . . . I will
bless thee . . . I will multiply thy seed . . . thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies . . . in thy seed shall
all the nations of the earth be blessed—four promises: (1) bless thee—give of His life to Abraham, (2)
multiply—the great nation of Israel, (3) possess the gate—rule over their enemies, (4) in thy seed shall nations
. . . blessed—Jesus Christ is this blessing. Because thou hast obeyed my voice—this is the condition. God's
blessings are given to those who obey Him. Israel lost possession of the gate of her enemies and was conquered
because of disobedience. All this Abraham did by faith (Hebrews 11:17).
Abraham's faith repeated itself in Isaac. Isaac trusted his father, knowing his father trusted God. He obeyed
in every move. To his question about the lamb, it was enough to hear that God would provide. He even took
without protest the binding and laying on the altar. He, too, had faith in God.
The line of faith has continued on in God's people. They which are of faith, the same are the children of
Abraham (Galatians 3:7). But without faith it is impossible to please him (Hebrews 11:6). Faith is not of
ourselves. It comes from God.

LESSON 7
A WIFE FOR ISAAC
Scripture Text: Genesis 24
To carry on God's plan for a nation, it was necessary that Isaac have a
wife. Abraham, a father with concern for his children, took steps to
obtain a suitable wife for him. He wanted the blessing of God's presence
to continue in Isaac's life as God also wanted (Genesis 17:19).
Abraham chose a wife for Isaac of his own people. Christ's bride, the
church, must be His own people. Rebekah was free to choose whether or
not to marry Isaac. God answers prayer. We are free to choose Christ or
not. Isaac took Rebekah to his own home. If we choose Christ, He will
take us to His home.
MEMORY VERSE: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also
loved the church, and gave himself for it.
—Ephesians 5:25
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 25:1-11 Isaac's inheritance.
Tue.—Genesis 26:1-25 God repeats His covenant to Isaac.
Wed.—Psalm 105:1-15 God's keeping of the covenant.
Thu.—Romans 9:1-8 Children of God reckoned spiritually.
Fri.—2 Peter 3:8-13 God calls all to repentance.
Devotional Reading: Ephesians 5:21-33 Isaac and wife a type of Christ and the church.
Of His Own Kindred
Genesis 24:1-4 Abraham said unto his eldest servant— Eliezer (Genesis 15:2) Put . . . thy hand . . .
swear—a custom in taking an oath binding a promise. We, as servants of God, are sent, as was Eliezer, to gather
a bride for Christ. That thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the . . . Canaanites. The Canaanites were
sinners, heathens, idolaters, not children of God, not fit for his son of promise who was part of God's covenant.
Go unto my country . . . my kindred, and take a wife for Isaac. She must be of his own kind. Christ's bride,
the church, must be of His kindred, have His nature, be born of God.
Had Isaac married a Canaanite, his home would have been built after a Canaanite pattern. The sins of the
Canaanites would have entered it. His children would have been half Canaanite. The lesson here applies to our
marriages. Young people, choose carefully. Your choice determines in large measure the character of your home
and of your own personal life. Do not marry the unsaved (2 Corinthians 6:14-15). Isaac's marriage is typical of
Christ and His church (Ephesians 5:25-27). He cannot have sinful people for His bride.
Isaac Not to Go to Haran
Genesis 24:5-9 If the woman will not follow . . . must I . . . bring thy son . . . unto the land from whence
thou camest?—go back to Haran among the people Abraham had separated from? Beware . . . bring not my
son thither again. It must not be. No undoing of God's work in separating a family for Himself. Refusal of the
woman to come to Canaan would release Eliezer from his oath.
To take Isaac back among a people of sinful, idolatrous habits would be disastrous. Then his family would
not be the pure, separated people God planned. So with us, Christ will not stoop to worldly standards in making
up the church. He will not take in a people who are not born again, whose hearts are still carnal, enjoying

worldly pleasures. Many of this class are members of denominational churches, but never the true Church of
God.
Some mistakenly think that to win the lost, we need to stoop to their level, do things and go places with them
so they will do and go with us. No, to do so would only weaken our witness. The Bible gives no encouragement
for this kind of actions. The world looks to the church to be different.
Lord God of My Master
Genesis 24:10-25 The servant took ten camels . . . went to Mesopotamia—the country where Abraham
stopped on the way from Ur to Canaan and where his brother Nahor and family stayed. He stopped at a well at
evening, when women came to draw water. He said, O Lord God of my master—he saw God's workings in
Abraham's life—send me good speed—give success.
He proposed a test by which to find God's choice. He would ask a young woman for a drink of water. He
asked God to cause his chosen one to give the drink and also offer drink for his camels. Rebekah came out—
Abraham's brother, Nahor's, granddaughter. Rebekah fulfilled the test. She . . . gave him drink . . . said, I will
draw water for thy camels also. God granted Eliezer's prayer. He brought Rebekah. It is God who draws us to
repentance and to Christ (John 6:44). Eliezer had faith in God. He prayed for guidance and followed it. Why?
Because he had seen faith and its answer in Abraham. What idea of God are people gaining from watching our
lives?
Bowed His Head and Worshiped
Genesis 24:26-61 The man bowed down his head, and worshipped the Lord—fitting worship and praise
for God's blessings. He blessed the Lord. There followed introductions to Rebekah's family, entertainment in
their home, explanation of his mission, and agreement that Rebekah should go to Canaan to be Isaac's wife. Wilt
thou go with this man? . . . I will go—it was her choice. We are free to accept Christ or refuse Him. It is our
choice.
Many ideas of worship are around us in the world. Some think that worship is in the quietness and beauty of
our surroundings. Others think that music, beautiful singing, etc., are worship. These may be associated with
worship, but are not worship in themselves. Worship is an attitude of heart. It is our answer to what God means
to us. When Eliezer saw God's goodness in answering prayer, his heart filled with thankfulness, praise, and love.
He just bowed his head where he was and let his heart pour out its thanks and praise and love to the Lord. That
was real worship.
Isaac's Bride a Type of the Church
Genesis 24:62-67 Isaac . . . took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her—a happy home
where love reigned, as God intends every home to be. The saints, Christ's bride, have fellowship with Him now
and are to enjoy the exceeding riches of his grace eternally in Heaven (Ephesians 2:6-7). We read in
Ephesians 5:25 how Christ . . . loved the church enough to give himself—His life—for it. Such love as the
Lord gave deserves the same love in return with our whole hearts.
Perhaps the greatest lesson in this for us is to see in it a picture, a type, of the church. As Abraham was very
particular in selecting a bride for Isaac, so God is in choosing a bride for Christ. If we would be His bride—and
we must be, or suffer the consequences of hell forever—we must be prepared according to His requirements.
The Church of God is not everyone and everything. It is a called-out, separated, purified, born-again, made-alive
people.

LESSON 8
ESAU SELLS HIS BIRTHRIGHT
Scripture Texts: Genesis 25:27-34; Hebrews 12:16-17
After twenty years Isaac and Rebekah had twin sons, Esau, the elder,
and Jacob, the younger. Jacob took advantage of Esau's weakness. The
devil takes advantage of our weaknesses. Esau sold his greatest treasure
for nothing. He would never be able to regain his birthright. It is a tragedy
to cast away our confidence in Christ.
When we are born of God, we have a birthright. We are heirs of God,
and joint-heirs with Christ. All of God's riches are ours. It is necessary
for us to look diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God (Hebrews
12:15). Jesus said, Watch. Value your birthright.
MEMORY VERSE: Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou
hast, that no man take thy crown.
—Revelation 3:11
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 25:19-28 Birth of Esau and Jacob.
Tue.—Obadiah 1-15 Esau's descendants punished for sins.
Wed.—Romans 2:1-11 God's righteous judgments.
Thu.—Hebrews 2:1-9 Neglect hazardous to receiving birthright.
Fri.—Hebrews 10:23-39 Great danger in casting away salvation.
Devotional Reading: Hebrews 12:14-25 Esau's tragic mistake.
Sell Me Your Birthright
Genesis 25:27-31 Jacob sod—boiled—pottage—a dish of boiled vegetables and meat. He was a plain
man, dwelling in tents—a quiet keeper around home. Esau came from the field . . . faint from hunting and
hunger. He was a cunning hunter, a man of the field . . . Esau said to Jacob, Feed me . . . red pottage—
probably made with red lentils, a favorite variety. Therefore . . . called Edom—Edom means red. The
descendants of Esau were called Edomites and his land, Edom. Jacob said; Sell me this day thy birthright—
the rights, advantages, privileges, and authority belonging to a person because of birth, especially, as in Esau's
case, the rights of the firstborn. This was an unreasonable price for a meal, taking advantage of Esau’s desire
and weakness.
Jacob cunningly took advantage of Esau's temporary weakness to take from him his most valuable
possession. Satan is ever watching for weakness in us to deceive and rob us of our salvation. He offers us his
cheap wares at a weak moment. He tells us our hope is already gone, and we may as well take what he offers. If
we listen to him, we soon find we have lost God out of our hearts. From every side, Satan tempts us to seek
pleasure from him, to serve self, to be discouraged, etc. Look carefully. See the real source of the temptation.
God will show us where our decisions will lead us if we will lean on and trust Him. Say no to the devil every
time. There is safety and help in Jesus Christ.
Despised His Birthright
Genesis 25:32-34 Esau said . . . I am at the point to die—this was obviously a great exaggeration. The
devil always causes our situation to seem greater than it really is. What profit . . . this birthright . . ? If he
should die, he could not use it. Jacob said —here is my chance—Swear . . . and he sware—bound his promise

LESSON 8
by an oath. He sold his birthright to Jacob. How cheap might you be selling your birthright from your Heavenly
Father? What did Esau receive for this precious possession? Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentils;
and he did eat and drink—it was momentary, it was soon gone. Rose up, and went his way—a way now
without a birthright. Thus Esau despised his birthright—set it at naught, disregarded it, and treated it with
contempt.
Esau is a type of those who cast away salvation for the empty promises of sin. He was discouraged. He felt it
of no use to keep his birthright. That is the lie Satan tells each of us. Discouragement always works to the
enemy's advantage. Discouragement is a treacherous tool of the devil. In a moment, Esau did something he
could not undo in this life or in the next. It is being done every day. One, in a moment of anger, takes a life and
pays with his own. Another gives way to greed or lust or despair and reaps sorrow for eternity.
If instead, one in a moment of hope yields to the Spirit's call and commits his soul to God, he will reap the
joys of salvation. If he then holds fast what God has given and goes forward, growing in grace, he will have
multiplied blessings eternally. Pray continually. Fear sin. Keep trusting God.
Found No Place of Repentance
Hebrews 12:16-17 Lest . . . any fornicator—one who brings something foreign into the place of that which
belongs—or profane person—with no respect for sacred things—as Esau. He was a spiritual fornicator and
profane when he sold his birthright. When he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected—when
Isaac gave Jacob the chief blessing (next week's lesson). He found no place of repentance—no way to change
it, it was too late—though he sought it carefully—remorseful now—with tears. Then he cried with a great
and exceeding bitter cry . . . Bless me, even me also, O my father (Genesis 27:34). Sad and tragic was the
realization of what he had done. His birthright was lost forever, and he could not change it.
The worse part of Esau's experience was that it was final. He had to suffer the consequence of his decision
afterward. We do not like to think of a time when any person can be past the hope of salvation. Yet at death, the
time to be saved is past, and sometimes one's act places the point earlier than that. To cast away one's confidence
in Christ, to say no to the Holy Spirit is very dangerous, foolish, and unwise. (Read Hebrews 10:35.)
Somewhere on that road is the point of no return. Tragic beyond words is the case of one who passes it.
Hold Fast
Revelation 3:11 When we are born of God, we have a birthright. God’s entire storehouse is opened to us. I
come quickly— Christ will return and then the Judgment. In view of that, hold that fast which thou hast—
never give up what you have from the Lord—that no man take thy crown—that crown of righteousness
which is to be the reward in Heaven for everyone who obtains it (2 Timothy 4:8). We must not lose it!
JUST A THOUGHT
Work is the yeast that raises the dough.

LESSON 9
JACOB RECEIVES THE BLESSING
Scripture Text: Genesis 27:1-38
In our lesson today Jacob, with the help of Rebekah, tricks Isaac and
receives the blessing intended for Esau. It is a dramatic story. Our characters
here were ideal people, but they had common weaknesses as we all do. None
sought God's help or an understanding of His plan. As a result, this whole
family was torn apart. A full reliance upon God's will and leadership might
have brought peace of mind, love, devotion, genuine happiness, and God's will
carried out as well.
The blessing brought with it special gifts of the fertile land, full victory
over all enemies, and superiority and rule over neighboring tribes and clans.
This made Jacob headman in the fullest sense. The blessing was automatic and
irrevocable. Isaac's faith enabled him to give a true blessing.
MEMORY VERSE: By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come.
—Hebrews 11:20
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 27:35-46 Esau's hatred of Jacob.
Tue.—Romans 9:10-21 Jacob was already chosen.
Wed.—Isaiah 1:5-20 Jacob's cleansing need is as ours.
Thu.—Zephaniah 3:8-13 God saves His people from deceit.
Fri.—Genesis 37:23-36 Jacob deceived by his sons.
Devotional Reading: Galatians 6:1-9 We reap as we sow.
God's Plan
Genesis 27:1-4 Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim . . . he called Esau . . . I know not the day of my
death—but he felt that it was near. Take me some venison—Esau's hunting and cooking of venison had
brought a special closeness to his father (Genesis 25:28)—that my soul may bless thee—not his lips only. It
was to be a heartfelt, God-given blessing, his dying blessing. As father, he was the spiritual leader of the
household, its priest.
Jacob was God's choice to carry on the covenant which had come through Abraham and Isaac and was to go
on forever. God did not choose him because he stole the blessing. Sin does not bring God's favor. Jacob was
already chosen before he was born (Genesis 25:23). Thus it was God's will that Jacob have the place given him
in this blessing. He had His own way to place the blessing where He wanted it. We must remember that those
people were living before Moses' Law, and they had little direction from God. This happening fitted into God's
plan in spite of man's faults, not because of them. Had Rebekah and Jacob done right, God still would have
carried out His plan. But He turned their wrong to suit His purpose, as He always can do. Why did God not
reject Jacob because of his wrong? If God rejected sinners, no one would be accepted of Him, for all have
sinned (Romans 3:23). But in receiving, He cleanses them. Thank God!
The Trick
Genesis 27:5-15 Rebekah spake unto Jacob . . . I heard—the plan did not suit her, for she loved Jacob
best—he stayed close to home, no doubt accounting for the special closeness to his mother. Fetch . . . two good

LESSON 9
kids of the goats; and I will make . . . savory meat . . . thou shalt bring it to thy father . . . that he may
bless thee—a bold scheme, a wicked deception.
Was Jacob's action right? It included selfishness, deception, and lying. These are never right. Even though
his mother came up with the scheme and encouraged him, Jacob also was guilty, as all of us are responsible for
our choices and acts. The moment our hearts consent to the wrong, we share the guilt.
He Blessed Him
Genesis 27:16-29 She put the skins . . . upon his hands, and . . . neck—to appear to be Esau who was
hairy. She put Esau's clothing on Jacob. In this disguise, Jacob took the food to Isaac. Jacob said, I am Esau . . .
bless me—he carried out his mother's scheme. He lied. It worked. He discerned him not . . . so he blessed
him. Isaac's blessing promised plenty of good things, that the people and nations would serve him, and he would
be lord over his brethren—be master and ruler.
Isaac's blessing was a true blessing. It was from God. It was beyond Isaac's power to make it. After he gave
it, it was beyond his power to change it. The transaction was legal and binding. Isaac could only say, "Yea, and
he shall be blessed."
Faith was the line by which Isaac brought the blessing from God. (See Memory Verse.) He did not know in
his own mind what to say. He, of himself, could not tell what was to come in the future. He did not make the
mistake of falling for this deception fully on his own. God had a part in the blessing going to Jacob. God had
said the eldest would serve the youngest (Genesis 25:23). Faith is not courage to face difficulties. It is not
imagination to see a beautiful ending. It is not optimism to look on the bright side. Faith is belief that reaches
clear to God and makes contact with Him. Through that contact, God told Isaac what to say. For that reason the
blessing was true. It was God's Word, and it came to pass.
A Bitter Cry
Genesis 27:30-38 Jacob was yet scarce gone out when Esau came. Did not God have a part in this precise
timing? The deception was uncovered, but too late. When Esau heard . . . he cried with a great and exceeding
bitter cry. Now Esau reaped from his act of selling his birthright. Because of that he really had no claim to his
father's chief blessing. Isaac gave Esau a blessing also, but it was less than that given to Jacob.
What sorrow and despair his cry, Bless me, even me also, O my father. Hast thou but one blessing? This
is a type of the final cry of everyone who sells his birthright, of every lost soul cut off from God. Esau CHOSE
that result the day he valued his birthright as one meal of lentils.
What a tragic state prevailed in this home because of the wrongdoing! Isaac's heart was broken and his plans
in disarray. Esau was hurt and enraged because of his foolish act that caused his downfall. He was angry with
his mother, his brother, and himself. Rebekah was a mother who had to stand back and see her family torn apart
and hear the shrieks of rage and disappointment and wild laments. It is a pathetic picture. Jacob took full
possession of all that mattered for the days ahead.
God has done all that is possible to save every person from such a fate. He warns us and waits, giving
opportunity after opportunity. He has made a way of salvation to all in the death of Christ. He has sent His
Holy Spirit to draw us to Him. The whole system is bound together in one. Hold on to your birthright, and the
blessing of the Heavenly Father will be yours.
JUST A THOUGHT
In our time, a wedding is where they take
each other for better or for worse—but not for long.

LESSON 10
JACOB'S DREAM AT BETHEL
Scripture Text: Genesis 28:10-22
After Jacob's treachery studied in last week's lesson, Esau
planned to kill him. To protect him from this, and also to find
him a wife of his own people, Isaac and Rebekah sent Jacob to
Haran to Rebekah's brother, Laban.
God appeared to Jacob at Bethel in a dream of a ladder
reaching from Earth to Heaven. Jacob yielded to God. He was
changed by the power of God. God renewed His covenant with
Jacob. Jacob was not chosen because he was good. He was
made good by God when ye yielded.
MEMORY VERSE: And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house
of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
—Genesis 28:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 28:1-9 Isaac sends Jacob away.
Tue.—Genesis 29:1-14 Jacob meets Rachel and Laban.
Wed.—Genesis 29:15-35 Jacob reaps his seed of deception.
Thu.—Genesis 30:22-43 God prospers Jacob.
Fri.—Psalm 51 A prayer for salvation.
Devotional Reading: Psalm 116 Vows paid in gratitude.
A Special Dream
Genesis 28:10-13 Jacob went out from Beersheba—his home—toward Haran. A certain place . . .
tarried . . . all night . . . took of the stones . . . for his pillows—a night in the open with the crudest of
comforts. He dreamed—a special dream—ladder . . . top . . . reached to heaven . . . angels of God ascending
and descending . . . the Lord stood above it—a way opened between Jacob and God. I am the Lord God of
Abraham . . . Isaac—a God familiar Whom he had seen in his father and grandfather, but unknown as yet to
Jacob. The land . . . to thee will I give it—the promise given to Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis
13:15-16; Genesis17:19), now repeated to Jacob who was to carry on the covenant.
God's direct speaking to Jacob was not an isolated incident. From Adam until the present is a series of such
communications, more numerous in the days before there was a written Word of God to guide mankind.
Repeatedly we read, The Lord appeared unto
and God spake unto
. Also, various ones inquired of
the Lord and were answered. As the written Word became more complete, the need for direct speaking became
less, but still, God speaks through His Spirit and His Word (John 14: 25-26; Acts 13:2).
Is there meaning to our dreams? God has spoken to men through dreams: Joseph (Genesis 37:5-10), Pharoah
(Genesis 41), Midianite (Judges 7:13-14), Solomon (1 Kings 3:5), Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2), Joseph
(Matthew 1:20: 2:22), Pilate's wife (Matthew 27:19), etc. He promised in this dispensation to send dreams to
some by the works of the Holy Spirit. However, these dreams will come very seldom. Most dreams mean
nothing. Dreams from God are clearly understood to be such and always are in accord with the Bible. It is
dangerous to attach meaning to our ordinary dreams or to go to those who claim to interpret dreams. So doing,
we can be led into disobedience to God and become entrapped in dealings of evil spirits.

LESSON 10
And I Knew It Not
Genesis 28:14-16 Thy seed . . . as the dust of the earth . . . in thy seed shall all the families of the earth
be blessed—again, the promise of a Savior to descend from him. Then a personal promise to Jacob—I am with
thee . . . will keep thee . . . will bring thee again into this land . . . will not leave thee. Jacob was a fleeing
wanderer, the future uncertain. God made it certain. Jacob would be returned to his homeland. Jacob awaked—
was the dream gone, meaningless as most dreams? No. Surely the Lord is in this place—the real presence of
God. I knew it not—he had not realized this before. He had never known anything personal from the Lord
before. The Lord had been near all the time, but he did not know it until now.
The Gate of Heaven
Genesis 28:17-19 He was afraid—healthy fear of God, and no doubt, a godly sorrow for the things he had
done in the past. How dreadful is this place! The great holiness, power, and glory of God overwhelmed him.
This is . . . the house of God . . . gate of heaven. Jacob rose . . . took the stone . . . set it up for a pillar—a
sincere, spontaneous act to worship the Lord for the great change which had taken place in his heart. Poured oil
upon . . . it—anointed it, set it apart as sacred. Called the name . . . Bethel—meaning "house of God." Its name
had been Luz; now it was a special place.
What happened at Bethel? Jacob was afraid. He remembered his sins and felt convicted. Here he yielded to
God. He accepted the Lord as his God. He gave a tenth of his possessions, a token of having given himself. He
testified to the change in his heart by the outward act of setting apart the pillar as a stake in his life, the place
where he first truly worshiped God. Jacob could not trust in Jesus' sacrifice to atone for his sins, for Jesus had
not yet died. But he did believe and trust God, which included all that God would later do. This was complete as
compared to the experience of justification which we can have now. He was now fit to enter into his place in the
covenant.
Why Was Jacob Chosen?
Genesis 28:20-22 Jacob vowed a vow—bound himself by a solemn promise. If God will (1) be with me
. . . (2) keep me . . . (3) give me bread . . . and raiment . . . (4) So that I come again—in short, if God did as
He promised in the dream, they were in business. Then Jacob made his promise (1) then shall the Lord be my
God—committed himself to God—(2) this stone . . . shall be God's house—a place to meet God—(3) of all ...
I will surely give the tenth—return of his possessions unto the Lord, realizing what he had never known before,
that it all came from Him.
Jacob seems to have had nothing to commend him to God as the proper one to carry on the covenant. His
past life showed cunning, selfishness, deceit, and lying. Why did God choose him? Because God was not
looking at his record as a basis for choosing. If God went by records, no one could be saved, for sin blots every
record. Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us (Titus
3:5). Jacob was chosen, not because he was good, but because he was willing for God to make him good. He
yielded to God and accepted His mercy. This story is written for our admonition.
Jesus saves the worst of sinners and places them into His great plan of work to help others to be saved also.
See Romans 9:16.
JUST A THOUGHT
Something else every couple should save
for their old age is their marriage.

LESSON 11
JACOB WRESTLES WITH GOD
Scripture Text: Genesis 32:24-31
Jacob wrestled with God to receive a blessing. God wrestled with
Jacob to cause him to surrender. Jacob's thigh was out of joint to take
away his dependence on self. He persevered to obtain God's blessing,
as we must too. God blessed him, and God gives us the Holy Spirit.
God gave Jacob a new name to suit his new nature. God gives us a
new name written in Heaven.
After twenty years in Haran where he had acquired two wives
(Leah and Rachel), two concubines, eleven sons and a daughter,
Jacob was called by God (Genesis 31:13) to return to Canaan. On the
way, the angels of God met him, indicating God's favor upon him.
Fearing to meet his brother, Esau, he prayed for protection and sent
gifts ahead of him.
MEMORY VERSE: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto
you.
—Matthew 7:7
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Genesis 31:1-16 Jacob plans to leave Laban.
Tue.—Genesis 31:17-35 Laban pursues Jacob.
Wed.—Genesis 31:36-55 Laban and Jacob part in peace.
Thu.— Genesis 32:1-23 Jacob prepares to meet Esau.
Fri.—Romans 8:1-17 Living in the Spirit.
Devotional Reading: Isaiah 62 The new Israel.
I Will Not Let Thee Go
Genesis 32:24-26 And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of
the day. Did you ever wrestle with God? Sometimes, the only way we can receive our blessing is to get alone
with God and wrestle with Him. When he prevailed not against him—the stranger did not overcome Jacob—
he touched the hollow of his thigh and it was out of joint. At first, the man used physical or human strength
only. Jacob was able to withstand that. The touch of his thigh was supernatural, and it weakened Jacob. He said,
Let me go . . . he—Jacob—said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. Now he recognized this as more
than a human man, as One with power to bless. Sensing this, Jacob was determined to have his blessing.
This is a type of how one must be determined to obtain salvation, to enter the Kingdom of God. Jesus said,
the violent —or the determined—take it (the kingdom) by force (Matthew 11:12). This world is a
battleground between God and Satan, each contending for our souls. God has made the way whereby each one
can escape from Satan to the safety of God's sheltering arms. But it cannot be done by fainthearted fearing to
act. The fearful will end up in the lake of fire (Revelation 21:8). Jesus teaches us to importune without giving
up (Luke 11:5-10). Read of the faith of the woman who came to Jesus determined to have a blessing for her
daughter (Matthew 15:22-28).
