LESSON 11
A New Name
Genesis 32:27-28 What is thy name? . . . Jacob. Jacob means supplanter. In telling his name, Jacob was
forced to lay bare the fact that he had taken the place belonging to another, had taken Esau's birthright and
blessing. Thy name shall be . . . no more Jacob, but Israel—meaning God's soldier, God's prince. God gives
names for the suitability of their meaning. For as a prince—as a victor, a successful contender—hast thou
power with God—to obtain answers to prayer—and with men—to lead and influence or conquer them.
His name would no longer be called Jacob, but Israel. Jacob won a place for himself, a place of his own. He
was now a conqueror, a victorious prince. Being a changed man, he was given a new name. This is a type of the
Christian. When one is saved from sin, he is made a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17). To him that
overcometh—sin and Satan, Jesus will give a white stone, and in the stone a new name written (Revelation
Only as granted by God can anyone have power. One of the wonders of God is that He gives His power to
work through righteous men and women. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much
(James 5:16). The secret of power with God is abiding in Christ. He said, If ye abide in me, and my words
abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you (John 15:7). God gives power with
men, the right kind of power, power to influence to do right, to lead to the Lord. The more complete the
dominion over our lives which we give to the Holy Spirit, the more He can use us as channels to influence
others.
He Blessed Him There
Genesis 32:29-30 Jacob asked . . . Tell me . . . thy name. It would appear here that Jacob strongly
suspected, yet wanted to be sure. Wherefore . . . ? And he blessed him there. In that blessing was Jacob's
answer. Whatever of comfort, strength, joy, new vision, and of grace entered his soul in that blessing, whatever
of the life of God entered into him then, it answered his question more fully than words could have done. He
knew now, for sure, that this was God. Called the name . . . Peniel: for I have seen God face to face. It
surprised him that after seeing God, my life is preserved, or spared. It is probable that God's glory was
somewhat veiled from Jacob, that he had but a partial view of His face. Consider Exodus 33:18-23.
God has often answered a question by action rather than words. A demonstration is better than an
explanation. See how God answered questions for Pharaoh (Exodus 5:2; Exodus 12:29-31; for Nebuchadnezzar
(Daniel 3:15, 28, and 29), and for John (Matthew 11:2-6).
Jacob Was Lame
Genesis 32:31 As he passed over Penuel . . . he halted upon his thigh—Jacob was lame. He was to realize
his weakness, to know that it was not his strength which had brought victory—the blessing. It was a gift from
God. See the Memory Verse.
Jacob was crippled to show him his inability in his own power. The blessing was not wrought by Jacob's
power or ability, but by God's. Jacob had been blessed at Bethel; here on his way back home, he was blessed
again, and he would be blessed many more times in the days to follow. So we find it to be that way as saints. We
need God's blessings continually along the way that we travel every day. This world is not our home; we are
only strangers passing through but one time. We cannot expect help from citizens of this world.
JUST A THOUGHT
Times may change, but principles never do.

LESSON 12
JACOB AND ESAU MEET
Scripture Text: Genesis 33; Psalm 133:1
Jacob feared to meet Esau. Sin brings fear. Esau showed forgiveness
and generosity. His natural character seems superior to Jacob's. God does
not accept man's natural worth (his fleshly traits). God accepts only those
changed by His power. Jacob erected an altar where he settled.
Jacob, returning to Canaan from Padanaram, sent messengers ahead
to Esau to announce his coming and to seek Esau's favor (Chapter 32).
They brought word that Esau was coming with four hundred men. Jacob
was greatly afraid. When he left, twenty years before, Esau was
determined to kill him for having taken his birthright by deceit. He sent
several large droves of animals as a present to Esau.
MEMORY VERSE: Behold, How good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
—Psalm 133:1
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Psalm 27 Trusting God in time of trouble.
Tue.—Romans 12 The life transformed by God.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 1:18-31 The power and wisdom of God.
Thu.—1 Corinthians 13 The nature of love.
Fri.—1 John 4:7-21 The love of God banishes fear.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 5:21-26 Peace with fellow men required.
Guilt Brings Fear
Genesis 33:1-2 Jacob . . . looked . . . Esau came, and . . . four hundred men—a frightening sight to
Jacob, who knew Esau's reason for revenge. He put his children with their mothers in reverse order of his love
for them—handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and
Joseph hindermost. His favorite wife and son were put in the safest place.
The Wicked flee when no man pursueth (Proverbs 28:1). Jacob had reason to fear Esau, for he knew he
had wronged him. Since then, the Lord had entered his life, and he no longer desired to take from Esau. But he
had not seen him to establish a rightful brotherly relationship. Awaiting the meeting, Jacob suffered the natural
results of his wrongdoing. Sin always brings suffering. God's forgiveness wipes away the greater part of it, yet
some natural reaping remains. There is some of it left for us to take care of.
The Happy Meeting
Genesis 33:3-7 He passed over before . . . bowed . . . seven times— did all possible to please his brother.
Esau ran . . . how Jacob's heart must have leaped within him—embraced . . . fell on his neck . . . kissed . . .
they wept. Those tears, how different! Esau's joy at seeing again his twin brother. Jacob's, of great relief at
seeing friendliness instead of the hatred he feared, and perhaps, of the deep sorrow and repentance of his own.
He was thankful that time had erased anger and revenge from Esau's heart. His inner fear had subsided. Esau
asked, Who are those with thee? Jacob introduces each group as it comes and bows. The children which God
hath graciously given—he considered them as blessings.

LESSON 12
To Find Grace
Genesis 33:8 What meanest thou by all this drove . . . ?—the animal gifts (Genesis 32:14,15). To find
grace—to win favor, to gain mercy. Esau could feel how deep and fervent was Jacob's desire.
Jacob could not come to Esau demanding his rights. By wrong action, he had forfeited all rights. He hoped
only for grace, that Esau would treat him better than he deserved. This is the way we must come to God—
seeking His mercy and grace. Sin has canceled any rights we may claim, but thank God! He has sent mercy. We
find abundant grace in Jesus.
Esau's Rejection
Genesis 33:9-15 Esau said, I have enough, my brother—tenderness, forgiveness, and forgetfulness are
here. Generosity was in his voice. My brother told Jacob that the breach between them had been closed. Jacob
said . . . receive my present . . . I have seen thy face, as . . . the face of God—the great relief in Jacob's heart
exaggerated Esau's kindness to a likeness of God's. Yet he acknowledged God as the cause of his blessings—
God hath dealt graciously with me. God had answered his prayer. He urged him (Esau), and he took it (the
gift). No doubt, both Jacob and Esau were sincere.
Esau was rejected by God as the one to carry on the covenant and to father the special nation to which Jesus
was to come. Had you and I been choosing, we might have considered Esau's generous forgiving of Jacob, his
cordial welcome, and unselfish treatment of him, and concluded that he deserved to be chosen. Indeed, he seems
to have a greater, natural bigheartedness than did Jacob. But God does not choose men according to their natural
worthiness or good traits. No one DESERVES anything from God. He has lumped all mankind together and
concluded all under sin, so all may receive of His grace (Galatians 3:22). The purpose of God . . . is to
stand, not of works, but of him that calleth (Romans 9:11). God looks not at how much of good or bad that
the person has done, but at how he responds to God's call.
In human judgment, comparing man with man, we think surely such a one will go to Heaven for his good
deeds and generosity. Yet if those deeds proceed from natural, human good nature, they are as filthy rags
(Isaiah 64:6). To be acceptable with God, one's goodness must be produced by the life of God within him. That
has a different quality. To be acceptable with God, our old man (self) must die, and we must become a new man
in Christ Jesus.
An Altar at Shechem
Genesis 33:16-20 Esau returned to Seir, and Jacob settled at Succoth. Built him an house . . . booths for
his cattle. His heavy burdens of the past wrongs were now gone, and he was ready to settle down and enjoy the
blessings which God had in store for him. Later Jacob moved to Shalem, a city of Shechem, in central Canaan.
He erected there an altar—continued to worship God. The name he gave it—Elelohe-Israel—indicates his
personal commitment to God. "The situation of the town is one of surpassing beauty. It lies in a sheltered valley,
protected by Gerizim on the south and Ebal on the north . . . It is the SYCHAR of John 4:5,6, near which the
Savior conversed with the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well."—Smith's Bible Dict.
Brethren in Unity
Psalm 133:1 Good and . . . pleasant . . . for brethren to dwell . . . in unity. This meeting of the brothers is
a much more pleasant picture than our previous views of them. Certainly, God was more pleased. His working
in the life of Jacob was a big factor in the change, if not its sole cause.
God wills that physical brothers live in harmony. A family bound together in love and unity is a beautiful
thing. Even more is it His will that His children, the Church of God, brothers and sisters in the Lord, dwell
together in unity.

LESSON 13
JACOB IN CANAAN
Scripture Text: Genesis 35:1-15
Jacob followed the leading of God. Jacob cleansed his family to
prepare to worship God. We must be clean before our worship is
acceptable. Jacob worshiped where God first appeared to him. It is good to
remember our experiences with God. God blessed Jacob again. God wants
to bless us if we will let Him.
Jacob realized that cleanness and holiness are necessary to please a
holy God. While he had continued to worship God since committing his
life to Him at Bethel years before, yet he had become somewhat slack and
allowed worship of images and use of charms in his family. To be fit to
meet God in worship, they must be rid of these. God accepts no mixed
worship.
MEMORY VERSE: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
—Matthew 5:8
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 45 The sin of worshiping images.
Tue.—2 Corinthians 6:14-18; Isaiah 52:1-11 To worship God, one must separate from sin.
Wed.—Deuteronomy 6:1-12 Saints' responsibility to pass on God's Law to their children.
Thu.—Ephesians 6:1-9 Parents and children relationship.
Fri.—John 5:19-29 Jesus example of father, son relationship.
Devotional Reading: Psalm 115 The sin of trust in idols.
Put Away the Strange Gods
Genesis 35:1-4 Jacob and his family had lived in Canaan for some time (since coming from Padanaram)
when God spoke to him in a command. Go up to Bethel. Make there an altar. Why there? Because there God
appeared unto thee when thou fleddest from . . . Esau (Genesis 28:10-22). The memory was dear to God as
well as to Jacob. He wanted Jacob to have the blessing which going back there would be. Jacob said unto his
household, and to all—he was responsible for those in his care—Put away the strange gods—images, idols,
probably brought in from Padanaram—be clean—morally clean from sin—change your garments—a physical
cleanness as a symbol of the moral cleanness. Let us go up to Bethel . . . make . . . an altar unto God, who
answered me . . . was with me—Jacob was remembering and measuring up to that mercy. They gave unto
Jacob all the strange gods . . . their earrings—earrings were put in the same category as strange gods. Why?
Because they were objects of superstitious trust to protect from evil powers, giving to them glory that rightfully
belonged to God. Jacob hid them under the oak—buried them.
He and All the People
Genesis 35:5-8 The terror of God was upon the cities . . . and they did not pursue—God protected Jacob
from the fierce people of Canaan. Jacob came to . . . Bethel, he and all the people . . . with him—took his
entire household into the worship. Built there an altar, and called the place El-bethel—an addition to the
name given before. El means God and El-bethel means the God of the house of God. The altar was a memorial
of the time God appeared unto him while he slept on the ground, when he fled from the face of his brother.
Jacob did not go alone. He included his family and servants in his worship. Are we content to worship alone
while the children go their own ways? Would we eat our fill while the family went hungry or sleep comfortably

in a warm bed while the children wandered in the rain and cold? The best of all blessings is to know God and to
worship Him in Spirit and in Truth. Let us not keep these to ourselves but do our best to bring them in.
God Appears Unto Jacob Again
Genesis 35:9-15 God appeared unto Jacob again . . . and blessed him. God came down and talked with
Jacob. We know this because he went up from him (verse 13). He repeated the promise made before of many
descendants and of giving Canaan to him and his seed, adding, kings shall come out of thy loins. The greatest
of these is the King of kings, Jesus. Jacob set up a pillar of stone, as he had done the first time (Genesis
28:18). He poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon—setting it apart as sacred to God.
After lingering at Bethel where Rebekah's nurse died, they moved on to near Bethlehem, where Benjamin
was born and Rachel died, to Edar, and on to Mamre—the plains of Mamre (Genesis 18:1) in southern
Canaan, to the city of Hebron. Here in Hebron, Jacob's grandfather, Abraham, had lived, and now his father,
Isaac, lived here.
Jacob's past experience was not enough. Its influence was fading until he was allowing images, etc., in his
house. He needed to be drawn back. He needed, as we do, a continuing contact with God. By continual prayer,
Bible study, fellowship with the saints, worship and service of God, our souls are kept flourishing, our love
fresh, our hearts tender, and our lives pure. Not what we were in the past, but what we are now is what counts.
He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved (Matthew 24:13).
Called the Name Bethel
One cannot meet God and ever be the same again. Always to be dear to Jacob's heart was Bethel, the place
of a permanent change in his life, the place where he first met God. God had led him to return to his land
(Genesis 31:13) and now to worship again at this place, this very spot. The ideal which had there been born in
his heart impelled him to cleanse his family of wrong practices to measure to the standard set then.
Let us never forget the God-stirred emotions which accompanied our salvation. Looking back to that time
and tasting again of that holy joy, many a one has been strengthened to overcome temptation, trial or
discouragement. The memory of that hour brings a renewed determination.
Jacob would later reap the seeds of deception which he sowed in his brother, Esau, through his ten older
sons in their selling of their brother, Joseph.
JUST A THOUGHT
It's a lot more fun to stop adding up your troubles
and to start counting your blessings.
